Fresh damages have been recorded in the Motor Vehicle Inspection Report of both the vehicles filed as part of charge sheet.
Perusal of the site plan shows the spot of accident and the path taken respectively by sctooterist and motorcycle just before collision.
This site plan was prepared at the instance of Rashmi Rana next day after the accident and has been filed as part of charge sheet proved on record as Ex.PW1/7 (colly).

It shows that scooty was coming from the left side and purportedly, took a big turn to move towards extreme right after crossing the chauraha on way towards Kali Market whereas motorcyclist was coming straight and collision happened at the spot on intersection (chauraha) where scooty had already crossed the major part and was just at a point to turn towards right while the motorcyclist was coming from their back and collided with the scooterist.
Further the spot of collision was farther away from the road from which side scooty was coming than for the motorcyclist.

Therefore, it appears that scooty had already taken turn and had crossed major part of the chauraha while the motorcyclist had better mean of vision to spot the turning scooter to avoid the collusion.
There is nothing on record about status of traffic signals on the chauraha to manage the emerging traffic from different sides of the cross road/ intersection.
It is evident thus that the offending vehicle was being speedily driven in rash and negligent manner thereby rammed into the accidental vehicle and caused death of one person and injured another.
Injuries sustained by motorcyclist in the process cannot absolve him of conclusion of act of rashness on his part while driving the vehicle on a public way.
As already stated, the scales of adjudicating rashness and negligence are way lower and lighter than one in the penal provisions.
Analysis of the entire evidence indicates that driver of the offending vehicle was negligent in driving, thereby caused the accident.

 disqualification of the driver or invalid  driving licence of the driver, as contained in  sub-section (2)(a)(ii) of Section 149, has to be  proved to have been committed by the  insured for avoiding liability by the insurer.
To  avoid its liability towards the insured, the  insurer has to prove that the insured was  guilty of negligence and failed to exercise  reasonable care in the matter of fulfilling the  condition of the policy regarding use of  vehicles by a duly licensed driver or one who  was not disqualified to drive at the relevant  time.
The Tribunals in interpreting the policy conditions would apply "the rule of main purpose" and the concept of "fundamental breach" to allow defences available to the insurer under Section 149(2) of the Act.

Even as per the guidelines issued by this Court Court, long term fixed deposit of amount of compensation is mandatory only in the case of minors, illiterate claimants and widows.
In the case of semi-illiterate claimants,
the Tribunal should ordinarily invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit.
But if the Tribunal is satisfied for reasons to be stated in writing that the whole or part of the amount is required for expanding an existing business or for purchasing some property for earning a livelihood, the Tribunal can release the whole or part of the amount of compensation to the claimant provided the Tribunal will ensure that the amount is invested for the purpose for which it is demanded and paid.
In the case of literate persons, it is not mandatory to invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit.
The expression used in guideline No. (iv) issued by this Court is that in the case of literate persons also the Tribunal may resort to the procedure indicated in guideline No. (i), whereas in the guideline Nos.
(i), (ii), (iii) and (v), the expression used is that the Tribunal should.
Moreover, in the case of literate persons, the Tribunal may resort to the procedure indicated in guideline No. (i) only if, having regard to the age, fiscal background and strata of the society to which the claimant belongs and such other considerations, the Tribunal thinks that in the larger interest of the claimant and with a view to ensure the safety of the compensation awarded, it is necessary to invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit.
Thus, sufficient discretion has been given to the Tribunal not to insist on investment of the MACT No.: 920/2021 Rashmi Rana Vs. Suprasad Gayen & Ors. Page No. 27 of 30 compensation amount in long term fixed deposit and to release even the whole amount in the case of literate persons.
However, the Tribunals are often taking a very rigid stand and are mechanically ordering in almost all cases that the amount of compensation shall be invested in long term fixed deposit.
They are taking such a rigid and mechanical approach without understanding and appreciating the distinction drawn by this Court in the case of minors, illiterate claimants and widows and in the case of semi literate and literate persons.
It needs to be clarified that the above guidelines were issued by this Court only to safeguard the interests of the claimants, particularly the minors, illiterates and others whose amounts are sought to be withdrawn on some fictitious grounds.
The guidelines were not to be understood to mean that the Tribunals were to take a rigid stand while considering an application seeking release of the money.
